name: Brunei Source Performance
title: GTCI 2025 — Brunei Darussalam: Performance in Original Data Sources (All 77 Indicators)
subtitle: Performance of Brunei Darussalam as reported directly in the original source databases that GTCI collects from. Includes source score, rank, trend, and detailed analysis.
rows: Government Effectiveness: Brunei scores ~80th percentile in WGI 2025. Reflects effective public service delivery anchored by a professional civil service. Limitations include low private sector participation in governance and limited accountability mechanisms. Civil service reform under CSPS and Wawasan 2035 contributing to stable scores.

Rule of Law: Brunei scores ~73rd percentile. Strong legal framework rooted in English common law tradition and Syariah law for Muslims. Gaps in judicial independence perception (no jury trials) and enforcement consistency in commercial disputes reduce the score relative to regional peers like Singapore.

Political Stability & Absence of Violence: Brunei's strongest WGI indicator — near-perfect score. Sultanate governance model, absence of political parties, and extremely low civil unrest or terrorism contribute. Consistent historically; one of the most stable countries globally. Key strength for talent retention.

Regulatory Quality: ~69th percentile — moderate. Business licensing has improved (Darussalam Enterprise reforms), but regulatory burden in non-oil sectors, FDI entry barriers, and limited regulatory transparency reduce score. ASEAN peers Malaysia and Thailand score higher. Brunei's regulatory reform agenda under BDCB and Business Licensing Centre is ongoing.

Corruption Perceptions: CPI 2025 (published Feb 2026) — Brunei scored 63, ranked 31st globally. Up from 60 (35th) in CPI 2024. Ranks 2nd in ASEAN behind Singapore (84). Brunei's Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) active investigations and asset declaration requirements contribute positively. Areas for improvement: procurement transparency and whistleblower protection.

Market Competition Intensity: WEF EOS 2025 score 39.42/100. Business leaders perceive moderate-low market competition. Oil & gas sector dominance, limited SME ecosystem, and few large domestic conglomerates create concentration. Wawasan 2035 economic diversification aims to create more competitive market conditions across manufacturing, halal, and digital sectors.

Domestic Credit to Private Sector: ~38% of GDP. IMF 2024 Article IV confirms bank lending to private sector rose 3.8% YoY in 2023 but remains structurally low. GTCI normalised score 15.42/100 reflects how far below global norms Brunei sits. SME financing remains constrained; BDCB credit guarantee schemes partially addressing gap. Islamic finance expansion could unlock additional credit channels.

Cluster Development: WEF EOS 2025 score 44.29/100. Oil & gas cluster (Seria/Kuala Belait corridor) is the most developed. Digital and tech clusters nascent — ITPSS (Anggerek Desa Technology Park) developing. Halal industry cluster at Pulau Muara Besar being built. Vision 2035 cluster strategy still maturing.

R&D Expenditure: Estimated at ~0.1% of GDP — far below UNESCO-recommended 1% minimum and ASEAN average (~1%). GTCI normalised score: 4.29/100. GII 2025 confirms Brunei's knowledge and technology outputs remain critically weak. No R&D tax incentive framework exists. UBD and BRUDIRECT-connected firms conduct limited applied R&D but no national R&D fund.
Population covered by at least a 3G Mobile Network

ICT Infrastructure: Brunei IDI 2024 score 95.1, ranked 2nd in ASEAN and top 30 globally. Internet access >90% of households. 4G/LTE covers 96%+ of population. 5G launched 2023 (DST, progresif). Fibre broadband expanding. GTCI 3G coverage score 93.09. Strong infrastructure foundation but digital services and skills utilisation lag connectivity levels.

Internet in Schools: Score=0 — Brunei not reporting this data to WEF. In practice, most Brunei government schools have internet connectivity (BDWAN network). Ministry of Education should engage WEF to submit national school ICT infrastructure data and ensure it is reflected in the EOS questionnaire responses from Brunei business leaders.

Urbanisation: Brunei urbanisation rate ~79%. High by ASEAN standards — reflecting small land area and concentration of economic activity in BSB. UN WPP 2024 is the most current data. GTCI normalised score 75.76. Urban concentration supports service delivery but limits agricultural and rural economic diversification.

Labour Rights: ILO ILOSTAT 2024 score 74.2. Brunei has ratified core ILO conventions but gaps remain in freedom of association (Trade Unions Act restricts union rights) and collective bargaining. Employment Order 2009 and its 2023 amendments strengthened worker protections. Migrant worker rights remain an area requiring further improvement.

Labour-Employer Cooperation: WEF EOS 2025 score 60.53/100. Government as dominant employer creates unique dynamics. Private sector cooperation improving under Darussalam Enterprise and BINA (Brunei Industrial and National Enterprise) initiatives. Tripartite Labour Advisory Board provides consultation mechanism.

Professional Management: WEF EOS 2025 score 60.63/100 — improving significantly (+18 pts). Government efforts to professionalise public sector management, CSPS (Civil Service Institute) leadership programs, and growing corporate governance culture in GLCs contributing to the gain. Sustaining this trajectory requires private sector adoption.

Pay-Productivity Link: WEF EOS 2025 score 46.51/100 — declining. Civil service salary structure insufficiently tied to performance outputs. Private sector productivity incentives limited. Performance management reform in public service (Penilaian Kerja Tahunan system) needs modernisation to tie remuneration more directly to measurable outcomes.

Enterprise Software Adoption: Statista estimates Brunei enterprise software market at ~USD 2-3M total. Per-capita spend among the lowest globally. GTCI score 11.86/100. Dominance of public sector (where software procurement is centralised) suppresses commercial market signals. SMEs largely operate without ERP/CRM systems. National digitalisation grants needed urgently.

Cloud Computing Adoption: Brunei public cloud market nascent — GTCI score 4.79/100. Government agencies beginning cloud migration (AITI cloud strategy). Private sector adoption hindered by data sovereignty concerns, limited local cloud infrastructure, and lack of cloud-competent workforce. National Cloud-First Policy needed with sovereign cloud procurement guidelines.

Business Sophistication (WBES): Score=0 — Brunei last surveyed by World Bank Enterprise Survey in 2015. Data gap means practices around training, corruption, finance access, and competition are not benchmarked. WBES 2025/2026 regional cycle is an opportunity; Ministry of Finance/Economy should formally request Brunei's inclusion. A Brunei-specific business climate survey could bridge the gap.

FDI Openness: OECD FDI Restrictiveness Index 2024 — Brunei maintains restrictions in financial services, media, and land ownership for foreigners. GTCI score 54.68/100. Despite Brunei's efforts through IPA (Investment Promotions Act) and IPA office, actual FDI inflows remain concentrated in O&G. Reducing restrictions in services and tech sectors could unlock new FDI streams.

Financial Globalisation: KOF 2025 update (covering 2023 data) available. Brunei's financial globalisation score reflects international banking ties (CIMB, BOC, HSBC presence), foreign asset/liability positions, and BIA (Brunei Investment Agency) sovereign wealth fund international portfolio. KOF captures both de facto and de jure aspects of globalisation.

Migrant Stock: UN Migrant Stock 2024 — Brunei has ~31% of population as migrants (one of highest shares in ASEAN). However, GTCI normalised score of 49.5 declined by 29 points. Recent tightening of expatriate employment permits and Bruneianisation (Local Business Development Authority) policies may be reducing migrant stock. Rebalancing towards skilled migration could improve score while supporting Wawasan 2035.

International Students: UNESCO UIS — Brunei attracts very few international students. GTCI score 15.76. UBD has some ASEAN Exchange Program students but absolute numbers small. Tuition fees and English-language programs are competitive but scholarship availability for international students is limited. A formal international student attraction strategy (target: 5,000 international students by 2030) could substantially improve this indicator.

Brain Gain (Talent Attraction): WEF EOS 2025 — Brunei ranks 16th globally on perceived talent attraction. Strong brand as a safe, prosperous, and culturally rich destination resonates with skilled expatriates, particularly from ASEAN, South Asia, and the Philippines. Tax-free income, subsidised fuel and utilities, and stable employment conditions are key draw factors. Opportunity to leverage this brand more actively in global talent recruitment.

AI Skills Migration: LinkedIn Economic Graph 2024 — Brunei not covered. Indicator measures net migration of AI-skilled professionals via LinkedIn platform data. Brunei's LinkedIn penetration is moderate but AI-specific talent movement data is unavailable for this small market. Ministry of Transport & Infocommunications (MTIC)/AITI should engage LinkedIn Economic Graph team for Brunei data inclusion.
Fund for Peace Fragile States Index 2024

Group Grievances / Minority Tolerance: FSI 2024 (May 2024) — Brunei Group Grievances sub-indicator at 27.66. Reflects perceptions around treatment of religious minorities (non-Muslims represent ~33% of population), rights of non-citizens, and ethnic minority recognition. FSI uses triangulated data from media, reports, and expert assessment. Brunei's MIB (Melayu Islam Beraja) national philosophy creates structural tensions with minority inclusion indicators.

Tolerance of Immigrants (Gallup): Score=0 — Brunei last included in Gallup fieldwork ~2020. Actual public tolerance levels in Brunei are unmeasured by this global benchmark. Given the ~31% migrant population, tolerance attitudes are important for social cohesion. Ministry of Home Affairs could commission an annual national perception survey using Gallup-compatible methodology to build a data series for GTCI submission.

Social Mobility: WEF EOS 2025 score 60.68 — improving significantly (+24 pts). Brunei's welfare state model (free healthcare, subsidised housing, universal education scholarships) supports upward social mobility. Government scholarship programs (MKMA, JPA, BESERAH) enable children from all backgrounds to access higher education. Wawasan 2035 social equity targets reinforcing this trend.
World Bank Women, Business and the Law 2024

Gender Economic Empowerment (WBL): WBL 2024 score 53.12/100 (rank 126/190). WBL 2.0 breakdown: Legal Frameworks 35.0, Supportive Frameworks 24.2, Expert Opinions 91.3. Low scores in Mobility, Workplace, Marriage and Parenthood dimensions. Key gaps: no equal pay legislation, limited maternity leave mandates in private sector, restrictions on women's property rights. WBL 2026 expected March 2026. Expert opinion (91.3) far exceeds legal score (35.0) — suggesting practice ahead of law.

Gender Parity in High-Skilled Jobs: ILO ILOSTAT 2024-2025 — Brunei women constitute a strong share of professional and managerial workforce. Brunei LFS 2024 confirms female workers account for ~85% of medium and high-skill occupational categories. Strong female participation in education, healthcare, and government sectors. Private sector female leadership less prominent but improving.

Women in Leadership: WEF EOS 2025 — Brunei ranks 28th globally (rank 28 out of 134). Senior female public servants, female HM Appointees to LegCo, and prominent women in education and healthcare leadership contribute to positive perception. Cultural and religious norms create some glass ceilings in private sector C-suite roles. Rank 28 is Brunei's strongest social inclusion indicator.

Vocational Enrolment: UNESCO UIS 2023 — Vocational enrolment as % of secondary education is low in Brunei. IBTE (Institute of Brunei Technical Education) is the main TVET provider with 5 campuses. Total TVET enrolment ~8,000 students. Low relative to secondary school population (~30,000). Stigma against vocational pathways persists. Brunei Skills Development Centre (BSDC) and SPN21 TVET stream aiming to change this.

Tertiary Enrolment: UNESCO UIS — Brunei tertiary GER ~27% (2019 most recent confirmed). Extremely low despite top-6 spending per student. Root cause: many Bruneians study abroad (Malaysia, UK, Australia) on government scholarships; local university capacity limited to UBD, UTB, UNISSA, Laksamana, and Cosmopolitan College. Expanding hybrid/online programs and increasing local university capacity are critical levers.
UNESCO Institute for Statistics / World Bank

Education Expenditure per Student: UNESCO UIS 2024 — Brunei government tertiary spending per student is among the highest globally (rank 6). Full scholarships (MKMA, JPA), OS (overseas scholarship) program, and overseas sponsorships drive high per-student costs. Despite top-6 investment, quality outcomes in tertiary enrolment (rank 85) and research output do not yet match the financial commitment.

Educational Quality (PISA): PISA 2022 results (Dec 2023) — Brunei ranked 43rd among 81 participating education systems in combined Reading, Mathematics, and Science. Scores improving from 2018 baseline. Gap to Singapore (4th in PISA 2022) remains significant (~100 points in maths). PISA 2025 cycle currently underway; Brunei participating. Results expected December 2026. MOE curriculum reforms under SPN21 contributing to gradual improvement.

University Rankings: QS WUR 2026 (June 2025) — UBD ranked 367th globally, up 18 places from 385 (2025). Academic Reputation rose 32 places to 406th globally. THE 2026: UBD ranked 351st (up from 401-500 band). UTB entered THE rankings (601+) for first time in 2025. QS Asia rank: 78th. Two consecutive years of improvement post-methodology overhaul. GTCI normalised score 17.53 will improve with next update.

Business School Quality (MBA Rankings): QS Global MBA Rankings 2025 and 2026 confirm no Brunei business school is ranked. UBD School of Business and Economics (UBDSBE) offers MBA programs but lacks critical mass in research output, international faculty, and alumni network to qualify for global rankings. Pathway: partner with ranked international business schools (e.g., INSEAD Southeast Asia) for joint program delivery and faculty exchange.

Firms Offering Training: World Bank Enterprise Surveys — Brunei last surveyed 2015. Data on training practices by Bruneian firms is absent from global benchmarks. WBES 2025/2026 regional cycle. Ministry of Finance and Economy should submit a formal request to the World Bank WBES team for Brunei inclusion. Alternatively, BEDB/Darussalam Enterprise could conduct a national business climate survey capturing this metric.

Employee Development: WEF EOS 2025 score 62.24/100. Civil Service Institute (CSPS/INTAN) provides structured learning for public servants. Private sector L&D investment remains low — few large companies have dedicated training budgets. HRD-Corp equivalent (like Malaysia's levy-funded training system) does not exist in Brunei. Introduction of a skills levy system could incentivise private sector training investment.

Delegation of Authority: WEF EOS 2025 — Brunei ranks 26th globally (score 65.69). Business executives rate delegation practices positively. Flat management structures in some GLCs and professional services firms. Government-linked companies increasingly empowering mid-level management as part of corporate governance modernisation. Strong result for Brunei — should be showcased in employer branding.

Youth NEET Rate: ILO ILOSTAT + Brunei LFS 2025 (released April 2026) — Youth NEET (Not in Education, Employment or Training) rate improving. Employed population 220,400 (LFS 2025). JPKE employment support programs, HRD subsidies, and graduate placement initiatives reducing NEET rates. Youth unemployment remains structural challenge — particularly for non-degree holders in a credential-heavy labour market.

Virtual Social Networks for Business: WEF EOS 2025 score 63.5. High internet penetration (90%+) and smartphone usage support social media adoption. LinkedIn, WhatsApp Business, and Facebook are primary business networking tools. Formal use of social networks for professional development and B2B networking growing but not yet systematic. Digital business culture maturing.

LinkedIn Connectivity: LinkedIn Economic Graph 2023 data — Brunei ranks 35th globally in professional networking penetration among workforce. Higher than expected for a nation of 450,000. Growing use among graduates, white-collar professionals, and government officials. LinkedIn Talent Insights available for Brunei market. LinkedIn's 2025 data update will reflect further growth as younger Bruneians join the workforce.
ILO Social Security Inquiry / UN SDG Database

Pension Coverage: ILO 2024 confirms Brunei TAP (Tabung Amanah Pekerja) and SCP (Supplemental Contributory Pension) provide 100% pension coverage for all formal sector workers. All employed Bruneian nationals covered by mandatory contributory pension scheme. World #1 achievement globally. A key competitive advantage for talent retention messaging — Brunei offers comprehensive retirement security to all workers.

Social Protection Perception: WEF EOS 2025 score 50/100 — moderate and declining. Despite comprehensive government welfare programs (subsidised housing, healthcare, education, fuel), business leaders' perception of social safety net effectiveness is middling. Informal sector workers and migrant workers feel less protected. Communication of social protection benefits and broader coverage of non-citizen workers could improve this score.

Brain Retention: WEF EOS 2025 score 48.17 — improving. Business executives perceive talent increasingly choosing to remain in Brunei. Competitive salaries in O&G and government, subsidised cost of living, and quality lifestyle factors (safety, food, community) support retention. Awareness of overseas opportunities via social media creates competitive pressure. Targeted retention programs for high-skilled nationals studying abroad needed.

Environmental Performance: Yale EPI 2024 — Brunei scored 48.3/100. Performs above Asia-Pacific average in water/sanitation and air quality. Below average in climate change mitigation (high carbon intensity from O&G sector), ecosystem services, and biodiversity. Brunei's Long-Term Development Strategy 2035 includes green economy components. Energy transition from fossil fuels critical to improving EPI score. EPI 2026 will reflect recent renewable energy investments.

Vulnerable Employment: ILO ILOSTAT 2024 — Vulnerable employment (own-account + contributing family workers as % of total) very low in Brunei (rank ~10 globally). Government is the largest employer; public sector jobs are stable and protected. Strong formal employment culture. GTCI score 95.02. However, migrant workers in construction and domestic work may be in more precarious situations not fully captured.

Workplace Safety Perception: LRF World Risk Poll 2024 (published Oct 2024) covers 121 countries — Brunei not included. WRP surveys ~125,000 people globally. Brunei's small population and limited survey participation explains absence. In practice, Brunei's workplace safety record (monitored by DOSH — Department of Occupational Safety and Health) is good. Engaging LRF for Brunei inclusion in WRP 2027 could secure a positive score based on actual safety conditions.

Financial Inclusion: Global Findex 2024 (Oct 2024) — Brunei not included in 123-economy survey. AMBD (Autoriti Monetari Brunei Darussalam) and BDCB data shows high banking penetration among Bruneian nationals but data not submitted to Findex. Ministry of Finance & Economy should coordinate with World Bank for Brunei inclusion in Findex 2027. Based on national data, Brunei account ownership is estimated >90% among nationals.

Personal Rights: Social Progress Index 2024 — Brunei not included in ~170-country index. SPI assesses political rights, freedom of expression, assembly, and movement. Brunei's MIB constitutional framework, absence of political parties, and press freedom limitations would likely result in a moderate SPI personal rights score if assessed. Government should proactively engage Social Progress Imperative to facilitate Brunei data inclusion.

Personal Safety: SPI 2024 — Brunei not included. Brunei is empirically one of the safest countries in Southeast Asia (extremely low crime rates, no street gang issues, low domestic violence reported). Royal Brunei Police Force crime statistics would support a high personal safety score if submitted. PDRM/Ministry of Home Affairs should engage SPI to secure Brunei inclusion — this is a missed opportunity to showcase a genuine national strength.
WHO Global Health Workforce / Brunei MOH

Physician Density: WHO GHO + Brunei MOH Annual Report 2023 — 1.87 physicians per 1,000 population. Below OECD average (~3.7) but above ASEAN average (~1.4). RIPAS Hospital (national referral hospital) and district health centres form backbone of public health system. Brunei relies significantly on expatriate medical professionals. MOH medical training intake expanding; overseas medical scholars on bond expected to increase physician density by 2030.

Sanitation Coverage: JMP 2023 — Brunei sanitation coverage near-universal (98%+). Safely managed sanitation and clean water access are exemplary — consistent top-5 global performance. All urban areas and most rural areas connected to piped water and sewerage. One of Brunei's strongest social infrastructure achievements. Relevant for "Retain" pillar quality-of-life messaging in talent attraction campaigns.

Employee Wellbeing: Gallup World Poll Wellbeing module — Brunei not covered. Score=0. Gallup's global wellbeing surveys require representative national samples with in-country fieldwork partners. Brunei's wellbeing is understood to be high based on national surveys (high life satisfaction, low stress indicators). Ministry of Finance Statistics Department could commission a National Wellbeing Survey using Gallup-compatible methodology to build a data series for future GTCI submissions.

Workforce Secondary Education: ILOSTAT + LFS 2025 — Workforce with secondary education as % declining in Brunei. Score 62.63 (-10.6 pts). This seemingly counterintuitive decline reflects a compositional shift: younger cohorts with tertiary education are replacing older secondary-educated workers, temporarily reducing the secondary-only share. The trend is actually positive — indicating upskilling — but appears as a decline in this specific metric.

Population Secondary Education Attainment (25+): ILOSTAT 2025 — 63.94% of Brunei population aged 25+ has at least secondary education. Improving as younger, better-educated cohorts age into the 25+ demographic. Government investment in universal secondary education through SPN21 system is yielding demographic dividends. Gap to Singapore (~85%) reflects legacy of lower historical education access.

Technicians & Associate Professionals: ILOSTAT 2025 — share of technicians and associate professionals in Brunei workforce growing (+6.9 pts). IBTE graduates contributing to this pool. Brunei Energy Sector demand for technical talent (petroleum technicians, lab analysts) driving growth. Growing demand in digital economy for network technicians, data analysts, and cybersecurity associates presents further opportunity.
The Conference Board Total Economy Database

Labour Productivity: Conference Board TED — Brunei not reported. Score=0. TED covers ~75 major economies. Brunei's labour productivity (GDP per employed person) can be estimated from DEPS national accounts data: high due to O&G sector but unrepresentative of overall economic productivity. DEPS should submit labour productivity estimates directly to Conference Board for inclusion in TED methodology.

Finding Skilled Employees: WEF EOS 2025 — Brunei ranks 119/134 globally — worst performing GTCI indicator and worst in ASEAN. Business leaders report severe difficulty finding qualified local talent across IT, engineering, finance, and management. Structural causes: low tertiary enrolment, skills mismatch between education output and employer needs, over-reliance on public sector as employer of graduates, and limited private sector internship/apprenticeship pathways. CRITICAL priority.

Education-Business Relevance: WEF EOS 2025 score 60.78. Curriculum improvements underway (SPN21 reforms, IBTE industry alignment) but gap between graduates' competencies and private sector requirements persists. UBD Industry Advisory Boards attempting to bridge gap. Internship requirements for all university programs (IBTE mandate since 2022) contributing to improvement.

Skills Matching: WEF EOS 2025 score 65.7. JobCentre Brunei (JPKE) matching platform improving graduate-to-job placement rates. Brunei Skills Recognition Framework (BSRF) under development to standardise skills credentials. Private sector placement challenging due to salary expectation gaps between government and corporate sector. Expansion of apprenticeship programs recommended.

Educated Unemployment: ILOSTAT + LFS 2024 — Educated unemployment (graduates unemployed as % of educated labour force) low in Brunei (rank 48). Brunei LFS 2024: overall unemployment 4.7%. Graduate employment rate relatively high due to public sector absorption. However, graduate underemployment (working below qualification level) is a concern not captured in this metric — potentially significant in Brunei given public sector dominance.

Workforce Tertiary Education: ILOSTAT + LFS 2025 — 35.56% of Brunei employed workforce holds tertiary qualification. Growing as university graduates enter labour market. Below Singapore (~60%) and Malaysia (~45%). Accelerating tertiary enrolment and retaining overseas graduates are key levers. Government overseas scholarship graduates (bonded) are increasingly returning and entering workforce.

Soft Skills: WEF EOS 2024 (note: GTCI 2025 uses 2024 EOS for this indicator; 2025 EOS will feed GTCI 2026) — score 57.13. Communication, critical thinking, creativity, adaptability among Brunei workers rated moderate. SPN21 curriculum reform targets 21st-century competencies. Private sector cites soft skills (particularly communication in English and problem-solving) as key gap among fresh graduates. Language skills development critical.

Professionals in Workforce: ILOSTAT + WDI 2025 — Professionals (ISCO major group 2) as % of Brunei workforce at 33.81. Healthcare professionals, educators, and engineers dominant. IT professionals growing from small base. Brunei's small total workforce (~222,000) limits absolute numbers. Diversification of professional categories through DART Digital Economy and healthcare expansion programs will increase this ratio.

Researcher Density: GII 2025 (Sep 2025) — Brunei researcher FTE density extremely low (0.2-0.3 per 1,000 labour force; GTCI normalised score 4.82, rank 73). GII 2025 confirms Brunei ranked 88th overall with continued weakness in knowledge outputs. Without researchers, R&D output and IP generation remain minimal. Establishing a Brunei Research Council, creating competitive researcher salaries, and introducing researcher visa pathways are essential.

Senior Officials & Managers: ILOSTAT + WDI 2025 — Senior officials and managers as % of workforce ranks Brunei 14th globally. Bruneians occupy large share of managerial roles across public sector, GLCs, and some private firms. Bumiputra Malay business ownership policy (local content requirements) ensures Bruneian management presence. Private sector management quality improvements underway through CSPS leadership programs and MBA scholarship graduates.

Digital Skills (ITU): ITU IDI 2024 — Brunei scored 95.1, ranked 2nd in ASEAN. 2025 IDI published. GTCI normalised score: 100/100. Note: the perfect score may reflect ITU's ICT access/use proxy for digital skills rather than directly measuring user competency. Brunei's strong connectivity infrastructure (5G, fibre) drives IDI score but actual digital skills competency (measured by OECD PIAAC or national digital literacy assessments) may differ. A national digital skills assessment would provide clearer evidence.
LinkedIn Economic Graph / OECD AI Policy Observatory

AI Talent Concentration: New indicator in GTCI 2025. Brunei not covered. Measures share of AI-skilled professionals as % of workforce via LinkedIn data. Brunei's AI talent ecosystem is nascent: AITI's DART Digital Economy Masterplan (2025-2030) includes AI competency development targets. University AI courses at UBD and UTB launching 2025. LinkedIn engagement and AI upskilling programs will be essential to appear in future versions of this indicator.

ICT Services Exports: WTO Trade Stats + GII 2025 — Brunei ICT services exports extremely low (GTCI score 2.44, rank 112/134). Brunei's export base remains >90% dominated by LNG and crude oil. ICT services (software, IT consulting, digital services, BPO) represent <1% of service exports. GII 2025 ranks Brunei 124th in Creative Outputs. Deliberate ICT export diversification policy — targeting ASEAN digital services market — is the primary lever.
Sensor Tower / data.ai via WIPO GII 2025

Mobile App Development: GII 2025 via Sensor Tower data — Brunei at 43.27/100 (moderate). Some local app development activity but limited commercial scale. Government apps (BruHealth, SALPOP) well-adopted domestically. Gaming, fintech, and e-government apps being developed. DART Digital Economy Masterplan encourages app ecosystem growth through AppSprint and StartUp Brunei competitions.

IP Receipts: IMF BOP 2024 confirms Brunei reports zero intellectual property receipts. No royalties, licensing fees, or patent income earned from abroad. WIPO GII 2025 ranks Brunei 124th in Creative Outputs. Reflects absence of IP-generating industries. Brunei Intellectual Property Office (BruIPO) established 2012 but patent filing rates remain extremely low. Introduction of IP tax incentives (Patent Box regime) and commercialisation support for UBD/UTB research outputs are critical.

High-Value Exports: UN Comtrade + WDI 2024 — High-value exports (medium-high tech manufacturing + ICT + knowledge-intensive services) represent <5% of total Brunei exports. O&G dominance constrains export complexity (Economic Complexity Index: Brunei rank ~120). GII 2025: Brunei 115th in Knowledge & Technology Outputs. Halal food and cosmetics export value chain, precision engineering, and digital services are priority diversification targets under BEDB's sector development programs.

Software Development: GitHub data via GII 2025 — Brunei software development activity minimal (score 3.02). GitHub commits per capita extremely low. Local developer community small but growing — BruDev community, BruHack hackathon series, and AITI coding bootcamps nurturing talent. Open-source contributions and startup tech products slowly emerging. DART targets doubling tech startup numbers by 2028.

New Business Density: World Bank Entrepreneurship Database — Brunei last reported 2022; score=0 in GTCI 2025. CRITICAL DATA ACTION: Brunei ROCBN registered 6,570 new enterprises in 2023 and estimated 7,200+ in 2024. This data must be submitted to the World Bank Entrepreneurship Database before GTCI 2026 data cutoff. Ministry of Finance & Economy / ROCBN should contact World Bank for urgent data submission. This single action could significantly improve Brunei's rank in the Growth (Grow) pillar.
UNESCO Science Report / Scopus / Web of Science

Scientific Publications: Scopus/SCImago 2024 + UNESCO Science Report — Brunei scientific publications growing; rank 37/134 globally (+8.62 pts improvement). UBD driving publication output through research institutes (CIBM, ISLB, IEE). UTB and UNISSA also contributing. Nature Index 2025 shows UBD rising in health sciences. International collaboration (with UK, Australia, Malaysia) boosting citation impact. Target: maintain rank improvement with sustained research investment and open-access publication policy.

ROCBN registered 6,570 new enterprises in 2023 and ~7,200 in 2024. Submitting this data to the World Bank Entrepreneurship Database is the single most impactful easy fix available. Ministry of Home Affairs / Department of Statistics

Gallup Tolerance of Immigrants: Brunei has ~31% migrant population — actual tolerance attitudes are unknown in global benchmarks because Gallup does not survey Brunei. Alternatively, request Gallup include Brunei in their rolling survey programme.

QS Global MBA and Business Masters Rankings 2025

Joint programmes can qualify for ranking consideration within 3-5 years.
Missing – Not in Gallup Wellbeing Survey

Department of Statistics (DEPS) / Ministry of Finance

Gallup World Poll Employee Wellbeing: Brunei not surveyed. National wellbeing likely high based on quality of life indicators. Cost: ~BND 50,000-100,000 annually for a proper national survey.

LinkedIn Economic Graph

AITI should engage LinkedIn Economic Graph and OECD AI Policy Observatory to ensure Brunei AI workforce data is captured. As AI upskilling programs mature under DART, this score will naturally improve.

IMF Balance of Payments Statistics / WTO Trade Database

IP Receipts: Score=0 because Brunei genuinely earns zero IP income from abroad. This is a structural issue, not a data gap. However, BruIPO should accelerate patent filing support for UBD/UTB research outputs and introduce a Patent Box tax incentive regime to attract IP holding companies to domicile in Brunei. Medium-term fix (5-10 years).

name: Granular Improvement Actions
title: BRUNEI GTCI 2025 — GRANULAR IMPROVEMENT ACTION PLAN: All 77 Indicators
subtitle: Detailed, step-by-step improvement actions for every GTCI indicator — including exact data submission contacts, engagement protocols, policy reforms, responsible ministries, and timelines. Colour: 🔴 Critical | 🟠 Weak | 🟡 Moderate | 🟢 Good | ✅ Excellent
headers: GRANULAR IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS (How to join source, submit data, contact details, step-by-step process)
rows:
SOURCE: World Bank WGI — Government Effectiveness. Brunei already included. WGI draws from 30+ underlying sources.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. BERTELSMANN BTI: PMO to send annual governance reform brief to bti@bertelsmann-stiftung.de each January — BTI Country Reports directly feed WGI. Request pre-publication review meeting.
2. EIU ENGAGEMENT: PMO to brief EIU Brunei country analyst annually — provide evidence of civil service reform, e-government progress, regulatory improvements.
3. E-GOVERNMENT INDEX (EGDI): AITI to submit Brunei EGDI self-assessment to UN DESA (egov@un.org) annually — directly feeds WGI Government Effectiveness.
4. CIVIL SERVICE KPI REPORT: CSPS to publish annual Civil Service Performance Report with measurable KPIs (service delivery times, citizen satisfaction scores, digital service adoption rates).
5. WGI TEAM DIALOGUE: Contact World Bank Governance Global Practice (wbgdg@worldbank.org) for annual country dialogue.
RESPONSIBLE: PMO / CSPS / AITI. TIMELINE: 12–24 months.

SOURCE: World Bank WGI — Rule of Law. Draws from WJP, EIU, Heritage Foundation, PRS ICRG.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. WJP RULE OF LAW INCLUSION: AGC to contact info@worldjusticeproject.org — request Brunei inclusion in WJP annual survey (surveys lawyers + general public in 140+ countries). WJP score directly feeds WGI Rule of Law.
2. PUBLISH JUDICIAL STATISTICS REPORT: AGC to publish annual Brunei Judiciary Statistics (case clearance rates, enforcement times, arbitration outcomes) — feeds EIU legal framework assessment.
3. HERITAGE FOUNDATION: Submit Brunei legal reform updates to heritage@heritage.org for annual Index of Economic Freedom survey.
4. PRS ICRG RATING: Ministry of Finance to engage PRS Group (prsgroup.com) for updated Brunei country risk rating.
5. STRENGTHEN BIAC: Publish Brunei International Arbitration Centre case statistics — signals judicial independence.
RESPONSIBLE: AGC / Ministry of Finance. TIMELINE: 12–18 months.

SOURCE: World Bank WGI — Political Stability. Score near-perfect (~98th percentile). Protect and leverage.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. ACLED VERIFICATION: Verify Brunei is coded "No Events" in ACLED (acleddata.com) each year. Contact ACLED data team to confirm.
2. EIU ANNUAL BRIEF: PMO to provide EIU Brunei country analyst with annual security brief — ensures EIU political stability assessment remains accurate.
3. LEVERAGE IN TALENT MARKETING: "Brunei ranks top-5 globally in Political Stability" — feature in all BEDB talent attraction materials and investment pitches.
4. INSEAD BRIEF: Proactively share this score with INSEAD GTCI team (gtci@insead.edu) to ensure prominent feature in Brunei country profile.
RESPONSIBLE: PMO / BEDB. TIMELINE: Ongoing maintenance.

SOURCE: World Bank WGI — Regulatory Quality. Draws from Fraser Institute, Heritage Foundation, EIU, World Bank B-READY.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. FRASER INSTITUTE: Contact info@fraserinstitute.org annually in March — submit evidence of regulatory reforms (licensing simplification, customs reform, price deregulation).
2. HERITAGE FOUNDATION: Submit annual reform evidence to heritage@heritage.org focusing on Business Freedom, Trade Freedom, and Investment Freedom dimensions.
3. WORLD BANK B-READY: Contact bready@worldbank.org — B-READY replaces Doing Business and directly feeds WGI regulatory quality. Brunei must participate formally.
4. REDUCE TIME-TO-REGISTER: Darussalam Enterprise to reduce company registration to <3 days (currently ~8 days). Each day's reduction improves B-READY and Heritage scores.
5. REGULATORY REFORM ROADMAP 2025–2030: Cabinet-approved roadmap with measurable milestones — signals commitment to all rating agencies simultaneously.
RESPONSIBLE: Ministry of Finance / Darussalam Enterprise. TIMELINE: 18–36 months.

STATUS: RESOLVED — Brunei now scored 63/100 in CPI 2025 (rank 31). Target 70+ by 2028.
HOW TO MAINTAIN AND IMPROVE: TI CPI uses 13 expert surveys. Key ones: EIU, WBG CPIA, BTI, WJP, PERC, IMD WCY.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. ACB ANNUAL ENGAGEMENT PROTOCOL: ACB to email cpi@transparency.org each September (before November data lock) with: ACB Annual Report, prosecution statistics, asset declaration compliance rates, new anti-corruption legislation updates.
2. ENGAGE ALL 13 CPI SOURCE SURVEYS: EIU (london@eiu.com), BTI (bti@bertelsmann-stiftung.de), WJP (info@worldjusticeproject.org), PERC (Hong Kong office), IMD (imd.wcc@imd.org).
3. BENEFICIAL OWNERSHIP REGISTER: ROCBN to publish public beneficial ownership register for all companies — directly improves TI transparency perception.
4. PROCUREMENT TRANSPARENCY PORTAL: Ministry of Finance to publish all government contracts >BND 50,000 online.
5. WHISTLEBLOWER PROTECTION ACT: AGC to draft standalone Whistleblower Protection Act — each new anti-corruption law adds CPI points.
TARGET: CPI 70 by 2028. Each 5 points = approximately 5–8 GTCI rank positions.
RESPONSIBLE: ACB / AGC / Ministry of Finance. TIMELINE: Annual cycle (September).

SOURCE: WEF EOS annually. BEDB coordinates Brunei participation.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. EXPAND RESPONDENT PANEL: BEDB to email eos@weforum.org requesting increase in Brunei respondent quota from ~50 to 100 executives. Provide curated list of 100 Brunei CEOs, CFOs, Managing Directors.
2. PRE-SURVEY BRIEFING: PMO Economic Planning Unit to host annual EOS Respondent Briefing (January) — 90-minute session covering recent regulatory reforms, market competition initiatives, and survey guidance.
3. MARKET COMPETITION REFORMS: Ministry of Finance to establish a Competition Commission with power to investigate monopolistic practices. Publish annual market concentration report.
4. BUSINESS LICENSING REFORM: Reduce business licence categories from ~80 types to <30 through a Licensing Consolidation Act — signals deregulation to EOS respondents.
RESPONSIBLE: BEDB / PMO / Ministry of Finance. TIMELINE: Panel expansion: 1 month. EOS impact: 12–24 months.

SOURCE: AMBD submits Monetary Survey data to IMF (statistics@imf.org) which feeds World Bank WDI.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. IMF SDDS SUBSCRIPTION: AMBD Governor to contact IMF Statistics Dept (statistics@imf.org) and subscribe to SDDS — commits Brunei to quarterly financial data publication. Ensures timely WDI updates.
2. COMPLETE MONETARY SURVEY: AMBD to verify IMF Monetary Survey (IFS reporting form) includes ALL domestic credit categories — ensure private sector credit breakdown is complete and not under-reported.
3. BRUNEI CREDIT BUREAU: Establish a national credit registry through AMBD — absence of credit scoring suppresses bank lending to unknown borrowers.
4. SME CREDIT GUARANTEE: BDCB/BIBD Development to launch BND 200M SME Credit Guarantee — government guarantees 70% of qualifying SME loans. Banks lend more; private credit rises.
5. SUKUK MARKET DEVELOPMENT: Ministry of Finance to issue annual government sukuk (minimum BND 500M) — develops benchmark yield curve, enabling private sector bond issuance.
RESPONSIBLE: AMBD / Ministry of Finance / BDCB. TIMELINE: SDDS: 3 months. Structural: 3–7 years.

SOURCE: WEF EOS annually.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. CLUSTER AWARENESS IN EOS BRIEFING: Prepare a one-page "Brunei Cluster Map" distributed to all EOS respondents before survey — show Seria Energy Zone, Anggerek Desa Tech Park, Pulau Muara Besar Industrial Zone, Salambigar Halal Park. Many respondents may be unaware.
2. HARVARD CLUSTER MAPPING PROJECT: Engage Harvard Business School Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness (isc@hbs.edu) for a Brunei Cluster Competitiveness Assessment.
3. CLUSTER TENANCY DRIVE: BEDB to fill vacant land in existing parks to 80%+ occupancy before next EOS survey — visible activity signals vibrant clusters.
4. PUBLISH CLUSTER ANNUAL REPORTS: Each cluster zone to publish annual performance report (tenant count, output value, employment) — distributed to EOS respondent panel.
RESPONSIBLE: BEDB / Darussalam Enterprise. TIMELINE: 18–24 months.

SOURCE: UNESCO UIS Survey on R&D (Form S). Submit to uis.stats@unesco.org. Deadline: June annually. WIPO GII uses UNESCO data automatically.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. FRASCATI MANUAL ADOPTION: DEPS to formally adopt OECD Frascati Manual as Brunei's R&D measurement standard. Train 5 DEPS statisticians in Frascati methods (training at stats.oecd.org).
2. COMPREHENSIVE R&D AUDIT: Map ALL R&D activities across: UBD research grants (research@ubd.edu.bn), UTB research (research@utb.edu.bn), government labs (BAFRA, EVPMO, IBER, BNRC), DST oil company R&D, private sector R&D. Many activities exist but are not classified as R&D per Frascati definitions — immediate reporting improvement possible.
3. OECD MSTI ARRANGEMENT: Contact STI.stats@oecd.org to request bilateral data sharing arrangement — OECD MSTI provides additional visibility.
4. PRIVATE SECTOR R&D TAX CREDIT: Ministry of Finance to introduce 150% tax deduction for qualifying R&D expenditures — incentivises companies to invest in and formally report R&D.
5. NATIONAL R&D TARGET: Cabinet to approve R&D spending target: 0.5% of GDP by 2028 (currently ~0.1%). Each 0.1% increase in R&D = approximately 5–10 GTCI points.
RESPONSIBLE: DEPS / Ministry of Finance / MOE. TIMELINE: UNESCO submission fix: 3 months. Structural R&D: 5–10 years.

SOURCE: AITI is Brunei's ITU focal point. Annual submission via ITU ICT Eye system. Contact: itustats@itu.int. Deadline: 31 January each year.
GRANULAR STEPS:

RESPONSIBLE: AITI / MTIC. TIMELINE: Annual submission: immediate. Coverage expansion: 2–3 years.

GRANULAR STEPS:

2. URBAN BOUNDARY REVIEW: Ensure DEPS's definition of "urban" aligns with UN-HABITAT definitions — some Bruneian areas classified as rural may qualify as urban under international standards.
3. PUBLISH URBANISATION STATISTICS: Annual Brunei Urbanisation Report ensures UN models use actual data rather than estimates.
RESPONSIBLE: DEPS. TIMELINE: Ongoing maintenance.

SOURCE: JTK (Jabatan Tenaga Kerja) is Brunei's ILO focal point. Annual Country Reports submitted to ILO Geneva. Contact: asia@ilo.org.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. ILO ARTICLE 22 REPORTS: JTK to submit all ILO Article 22 compliance reports on time every September. Missing reports reduce compliance perception in Labour Rights Index. Contact ILO Regional Office Bangkok: ilo@ilo.org.
2. RATIFY ILO CONVENTIONS: AGC/Ministry of Home Affairs to conduct legal feasibility study on ratifying Convention 87 (Freedom of Association) and Convention 98 (Collective Bargaining) — even ratification with reservations improves score.

4. DECENT WORK COUNTRY PROGRAMME: JTK to sign a Brunei DWCP with ILO — formal partnership ensures regular technical assistance and data quality checks.
5. OSHA ENFORCEMENT DATA: Submit annual occupational health and safety statistics to ILOSTAT under SDG 8.8 indicator framework.
RESPONSIBLE: JTK / AGC. TIMELINE: Annual reports: immediate. Convention ratification: 12–24 months.

SOURCE: WEF EOS annually.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. TRIPARTITE BOARD REVITALISATION: Reinvigorate Brunei Tripartite Labour Advisory Board (TLAB) — publish annual TLAB Report with concrete outcomes. Ensure EOS respondents know TLAB exists and is active.
2. EOS PANEL COMPOSITION: Ensure HR Directors and labour relations managers are included in Brunei EOS panel — they are most qualified to rate labour-employer cooperation.
3. SECTORAL COOPERATION COMPACTS: JTK to facilitate formal labour-employer cooperation agreements in top 5 sectors by employment (O&G, construction, retail, healthcare, hospitality).
4. DISPUTE RESOLUTION STATISTICS: Publish annual Labour Dispute Resolution Statistics — highlight Brunei's near-zero industrial action rate. Brief EOS respondents.
RESPONSIBLE: JTK / BEDB. TIMELINE: 12–18 months.

SOURCE: WEF EOS annually. Score improving (+18 pts) — sustain momentum.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. INSTITUTE OF DIRECTORS BRUNEI: Establish a Brunei Institute of Directors (BIoD) offering accredited corporate governance training. All GLC board members to be IoD-certified by 2027.
2. CSPS PRIVATE SECTOR COHORTS: CSPS to open Senior Leadership Development Programme to 20 private sector executives per cohort — cross-pollination improves perceived management quality.
3. PUBLISH GLC GOVERNANCE RATINGS: Ministry of Finance to publish annual GLC Governance Scorecard — transparency signals professional management to EOS respondents.
4. IMD WCY ENGAGEMENT: Contact IMD World Competitiveness Center (imd.wcc@imd.org) about Brunei inclusion in IMD WCY — IMD surveys management quality independently and provides additional credibility.
RESPONSIBLE: CSPS / Ministry of Finance. TIMELINE: 12–18 months.

SOURCE: WEF EOS annually.
GRANULAR STEPS:

3. PRODUCTIVITY INDEX PUBLICATION: DEPS to publish annual Brunei Labour Productivity Index by sector — shows respondents that productivity is measured and rewarded.
4. PRIVATE SECTOR FRAMEWORK: Darussalam Enterprise to develop Brunei Productivity Rewards Standard (voluntary) — companies linking bonuses to KPIs receive certification. Brief EOS respondents on uptake.
RESPONSIBLE: JPA / Ministry of Finance / DEPS. TIMELINE: PKT reform: 12–18 months.

SOURCE: Statista compiles from IDC, Gartner, and national ICT surveys.
GRANULAR STEPS:
1. SUBMIT NATIONAL ICT SURVEY DATA: AITI to conduct Annual National ICT Survey of 500+ businesses. Submit results to IDC (idcresearch@idc.com) and Gartner (datasubmission@gartner.com) for inclusion in their country models that feed Statista.
2. ENTERPRISE DIGITALISATION GRANT: AITI to launch BND 50M Enterprise Digitalisation Grant — co-fund 50% of ERP/CRM/cloud software costs for SMEs (max BND 50,000 per SME). Each grant generates measurable enterprise software spend in national statistics.
3. GLC MANDATE: Ministry of Finance to require all major GLCs to implement full ERP systems by 2026 and publish digital maturity scores annually.
4. ZERO-RATED TECH SPENDING: Introduce zero Business Services Tax on enterprise software licensing for SMEs — reduces adoption cost barrier.
5. ATTRACT TECH VENDORS: BEDB to offer 3-year rental subsidy for Microsoft, SAP, Oracle to establish Brunei country offices — their local presence generates country-attributed market revenue.
RESPONSIBLE: AITI / Ministry of Finance / BEDB. TIMELINE: Grant programme: 6 months. Market data impact: 2–3 years.

SOURCE: Statista compiles from Gartner, IDC, and national ICT surveys.

2. SOVEREIGN CLOUD FRAMEWORK: AITI to publish Brunei Sovereign Cloud Guidelines designating approved cloud regions. Removes the #1 barrier to private sector cloud adoption (data sovereignty uncertainty).

4. HYPERSCALER ATTRACTION: BEDB to formally invite AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure to establish availability zones in Brunei. One hyperscaler data centre dramatically increases cloud revenue attributed to Brunei.
5. IDC SUBMISSION: AITI to submit Brunei ICT Market Report to IDC (idcresearch@idc.com) annually including cloud adoption statistics — feeds Gartner and Statista models.
RESPONSIBLE: AITI / MTIC / BEDB. TIMELINE: Policy: 3–6 months. Market data impact: 2–3 years.

RESPONSIBLE: BDEPA / Ministry of Finance. TIMELINE: Questionnaire verification: immediate. Regulatory reforms: 12–24 months per sector.

RESPONSIBLE: DEPS / JTK. TIMELINE: Data: immediate. Policy: 6–12 months.

4. STUDYPORTALS REGISTRATION: UBD, UTB, Heriot-Watt Brunei to register all programmes on Studyportals.com (200M student visitors annually).
RESPONSIBLE: MOE / UBD International Office / JTK. TIMELINE: Data submission: 1–3 months. Student numbers: 2–5 years.
